title: Zero Data Retention: The Trust Threshold for Enterprise AI Inference
summary: Bitdeer AI treats Zero Data Retention as a core principle of its inference services.
body_markdown:
When enterprises evaluate AI inference services, throughput, latency, and cost per million tokens are easy to compare side by side. How a provider handles data is much harder to verify. API documentation explains how to call an endpoint, but it rarely says what happens to a request once it reaches the server: whether the data is stored, for how long, who can access it, and whether it is used for anything else.


As AI becomes part of core business systems, these questions are no longer theoretical. The prompts sent to models today often contain contract drafts, source code, customer records, and even internal credentials. Zero Data Retention (ZDR) has therefore moved from an item on a security questionnaire to a firm requirement in many enterprise procurement processes.


The problem is that providers do not all mean the same thing when they say they support ZDR. The sections below look at why ZDR is drawing attention now, what it actually covers, what recent security incidents have in common, and what buyers should ask when choosing a provider.


### **1. Why ZDR matters now**


First, the data entering inference pipelines is more sensitive than before. Early LLM usage centered on general Q&A and content generation. Today, agents search knowledge bases, read code repositories, and call internal tools, then pass all of that context to an inference service. Sensitive data is reaching inference services more often and in larger volumes, and much of it is assembled automatically without the user necessarily being aware of it.


Second, security incidents have become more frequent. Over the past year, discount API resellers have been found capturing customer prompts, some providers have routed requests to third-party models without telling customers, and companies have discovered internal code and production credentials passing to nodes they could not trace. Around October, a number of AI developer platforms disclosed further incidents, which are covered in Section 4.


Third, procurement and compliance requirements are tightening. Whether prompts are stored, whether data is used for training, and where data is processed have become routine questions in security due diligence. The storage limitation principle in regulations such as GDPR also requires that data be kept no longer than necessary for its purpose.


### **2. Understanding ZDR**


The definition of ZDR is straightforward: once a request has been processed, the provider keeps neither the request content nor the model output, and does not use either for training, product improvement, or any other purpose. In practice, several points are commonly misunderstood:


- **Not training on data and not storing data are different commitments.** Almost every enterprise-facing provider promises not to train models on customer data, but that does not mean the data is not stored. Some providers retain inputs and outputs by default for service optimizations such as faster inference, and stop only when the customer turns on ZDR. The first commitment limits how data is used; the second limits whether it is kept at all.
- **Not storing content does not mean storing nothing.** Billing, quota management, abuse prevention, and auditing all depend on metadata such as request counts, token usage, and timestamps. A well-written ZDR policy makes the boundary explicit: it records resource usage, not conversation content. A provider that claims to keep nothing whatsoever is worth a closer look.
- **Real-time inference is only one part of the product.** Real-time inference can release data as soon as a response is returned, but batch inference, video generation, stateful conversation APIs, and fine-tuning datasets all need to hold data for a period of time. Many providers apply ZDR to real-time inference only and list these storage-dependent features as exceptions. When evaluating a provider, check whether the list of exceptions is complete, whether staged data is isolated, encrypted, and subject to a retention limit, and whether it is actually deleted when that limit is reached.
- **When ZDR takes effect, and what happens to earlier data.** Where ZDR has to be switched on manually, it usually applies only to requests made after it is enabled. Data stored before that point is not removed automatically. Teams that turn it on after using a service for some time should confirm separately how historical data will be handled.
- **Where data is processed and where it is stored may differ.** Regional inference generally guarantees only that computation takes place in a given region, while logs, backups, and routing may be located elsewhere. Questions about data residency should cover the entire path, not just the data center where the GPUs sit.


ZDR is a requirement that runs through the whole pipeline and cannot be met by turning on a single setting. If any stage, including authentication, inference, storage, logging, or backup, keeps a copy, the commitment cannot hold.


### **3. Five shifts underway in the industry**


Looking at how enterprise inference offerings have developed in recent years, data governance is moving from privacy policy statements toward concrete mechanisms that can be verified.


- **Default activation is becoming the norm.** ZDR used to require a request or a manual setting. A growing number of enterprise-facing services now enable it by default. Since few teams review every configuration option, the default largely determines the level of protection most customers actually receive.
- **Architecture is replacing verbal assurances.** Security increasingly relies on limits enforced by the system rather than on providers' own statements. Customer-managed keys, provider operational access granted case by case, hardware-based attestation of infrastructure, and confidential computing are steadily becoming standard features of AI cloud and inference services.
- **Tenant isolation is extending to the compute layer.** Shared multi-tenant GPUs are what allow inference services to keep costs down, but they also introduce risks that traditional SaaS never had to deal with. Isolation therefore has to go beyond the application and database layers to cover compute and memory, so that data from one workload cannot be read by the next.
- **Data residency is becoming more transparent.** Where data is processed and stored, which sub-processors are involved, whether a Data Processing Agreement (DPA) is in place, and which legal mechanism governs cross-border transfers are becoming routine disclosures.
- **"No training" is moving into contracts.** Commitments not to train models on customer data or reuse it across customers are shifting from marketing language on websites to binding obligations in terms of service and DPAs.


Technical architecture limits what a system is able to do, while contracts and policies govern what a provider will do. Only together do they provide complete protection.


### **4. What recent security incidents have in common**


Security incidents involving AI development and inference platforms rose noticeably in the second half of this year. According to security researchers, at least nine AI developer platforms disclosed incidents in October alone. The entry points differed from case to case, but five common patterns stand out:


- **Credentials are the primary target.** In a number of incidents, attackers specifically searched for the environment variables and API keys customers had stored on a platform, particularly credentials that grant access to AI services. In cases tracked by researchers, attackers began testing stolen keys less than half an hour after the credentials were accessed. In one case, a stolen key was used to make about 1.7 million API calls in 13 hours. The cost to an enterprise goes beyond an unexpected bill: model calls are made in its name, entirely outside its control.
- **Stolen access ends up on the resale market.** Some stolen keys have been linked to services selling discounted access to AI models. The industry calls this practice of hijacking model access and reselling tokens LLMjacking. Unusually cheap API channels may therefore be running on stolen compute, and requests sent through them carry no assurance about where the data goes.
- **Stored data is the main point of exposure.** If real-time inference genuinely retains nothing, a breach can expose very little request content. What tends to be affected are features that store data, such as batch jobs, datasets, conversation records, and logs. How far ZDR coverage extends largely determines how much damage a single intrusion can do.
- **Intrusions often start at the periphery.** In several cases, the entry point was not the core inference system but a development environment, a third-party cloud service, or a software dependency. The more external components a provider relies on, the more weak points there are to exploit. Likewise, the inference services behind the SaaS tools employees use every day form part of the data perimeter an enterprise needs to understand.
- **Attacks are moving faster.** Some platforms reported signs of automated, large-scale attacks that sharply shortened the time between intrusion and exploitation. Defenses that rely mainly on manual detection and after-the-fact remediation struggle to keep pace.


These patterns show that ZDR is necessary, though not sufficient on its own. Enterprises also need to know three things: every system within a provider where their data has resided, how credentials stored on the platform are protected, and whether access can be revoked and rotated quickly when something goes wrong. Note that deleting a stored key from a platform does not revoke it; it has to be rotated with the issuer.


### **5. An overlooked factor: the length of the supply chain**


Most of the incidents described above share a common feature: between the enterprise and the underlying compute sit one or more layers of resellers, routers, or aggregators, or the provider itself depends on another cloud platform.


The main problem these intermediaries create is not latency, but a lack of traceable accountability. How many times was a request forwarded? Did each intermediary keep a copy? In which jurisdiction does the data ultimately reside? Who is responsible if something goes wrong? Every additional link in the chain adds another point at which a ZDR commitment cannot be verified. Some platforms also offer so-called passthrough models, which forward requests to external model providers for processing; whether ZDR still applies to those requests needs to be confirmed separately.


The LLMjacking described earlier is directly relevant here: stolen keys and compute end up behind illicit routing gateways and are resold as low-cost tokens. When enterprises call models through cheap channels of unknown origin, they can neither confirm which nodes their data passed through nor hold anyone accountable.


This is why more enterprises now distinguish between first-party providers and resale channels when making a selection. Only a provider that operates its own compute and network is in a position to make commitments about every stage of the path and to take clear responsibility when problems arise.


### **6. Ten questions to consider when choosing a provider**


**Scope and default settings**


1. Is ZDR enabled by default? If it has to be requested, does enabling it affect performance or features?
2. Which endpoints and features does ZDR cover, and which are exceptions?
3. If ZDR was enabled later, how is data stored before that point handled?


**Data retention and use**


4. What data is retained, for how long, and for what purpose? Are logs and backups included? 5. Is customer data used for training or product improvement? Are these commitments written into the contract or DPA?


**Processing path and data residency**


6. Are requests processed on the provider's own infrastructure? Are any forwarded to third-party models or cloud platforms?


7. In which regions is data processed, and in which is it stored? Is a list of sub-processors available?


**Access and credential management**


8. Under what circumstances can provider staff access customer data? Is customer authorization required, and is access logged for audit?


9. How are keys and credentials stored on the platform encrypted, and who is able to decrypt them?


**Independent verification**


10. Which third-party audit reports or certifications support these commitments?


Providers that can give specific, written answers to these questions generally hold up better under security due diligence.


Performance and cost determine whether an AI application can run; data governance determines whether it can be trusted in production. Just as HTTPS went from optional to standard for websites, ZDR is likely to become a baseline requirement for enterprise inference services.


Beyond that baseline, providers will be distinguished by three things: how comprehensive their commitments are, how clearly they disclose exceptions, and how short their service path is and how clearly accountability is assigned. Enterprise trust in a provider should ultimately rest on an architecture that is transparent, auditable, and clearly accountable, rather than on verbal assurances.


Bitdeer AI treats Zero Data Retention as a core principle of its inference services. Because inference requests are processed on Bitdeer AI's own infrastructure, Bitdeer AI can make commitments for every step the data passes through, and take clear responsibility for them. This lets enterprises access reliable compute and move their AI applications into production with confidence.
